unit.subtitle: Four siblings, two parents and the quiet revelations that crack open an Australian suburban family.

lessons.title: Plot and Structure: Four Seasons, Four Children
lessons.content_html:
A Year in the Price Garden

Andrew Bovell's Things I Know to Be True is structured around the four seasons of a single year. Each season belongs primarily to one of the four adult Price children — Pip in spring, Mark in summer, Ben in autumn, Rosie in winter — and each season delivers a revelation that unsettles the suburban family. This seasonal frame is not decorative. It is the play's dramatic structure: four interlocking acts of unequal emotional weight, building cumulatively towards a shock at the play's close that retrospectively re-orders what the audience believed they understood.

The structure is broadly chronological, moving through a calendar year. Yet within each season, time is not always linear. Bovell inserts direct address monologue passages, particularly through the voice of Rosie, who acts as a narrator-figure. These moments allow characters to speak from a future perspective, as if looking back on what the season revealed, creating a layer of dramatic irony that gives the audience information slightly ahead of the other characters.

Key Fact

The four seasons map onto four children: spring (Pip), summer (Mark), autumn (Ben), winter (Rosie). Each season brings a revelation that tests the Price family's sense of who they are and what holds them together.

The Kitchen and the Garden as Twin Centres

The action takes place primarily in two spaces: the Price family kitchen and the suburban rose garden Bob tends throughout the year. The garden is both a literal and symbolic space. As a symbol, it holds Bob's emotional life: his sense of order, control and beauty in a world where his children's revelations keep threatening to undermine the certainties he has built. On stage, the garden can be established simply — a few rose bushes, a soil patch, a garden chair — and the blocking often places Bob alone there before another character arrives to disturb his peace.

The kitchen, meanwhile, is the domestic centre: Fran's territory, associated with food, practicality and direct speech. In production, the two spaces can coexist on stage simultaneously, so that a director's choice about proxemics between characters moving between kitchen and garden becomes itself a staging language. When a child crosses from the kitchen to join Bob in the garden, the move marks a shift in emotional register.

A common student error is to retell the four revelations as plot summary. What lifts an answer is analysis of why Bovell chose this structure. Consider what the seasonal frame achieves: each revelation lands at a different emotional temperature. Spring carries the energy of new beginnings; Pip's departure is therefore against the grain of hope. Autumn's association with decay and harvest perfectly frames Ben's arrest. Winter's coldness amplifies the shock of the play's ending.

The structural symmetry also allows Bovell to make each child's season resonate against the others. The audience accumulates information across the year, so by winter they carry the emotional weight of every previous season. As a designer, you might reflect this accumulation through a gradually changing lighting palette — brighter, warmer in spring, progressively more stripped and cool by winter — creating a visual arc that reinforces the structural one.

Frantic Assembly Movement Within the Seasonal Frame

The play was co-developed with Frantic Assembly, the British physical theatre company, and their influence shapes where moments of stylised movement are inserted into the seasonal structure. At emotional peaks — moments too large for naturalistic dialogue — the characters enter Frantic Assembly movement sequences: chair duets, contact lifts and round-by-through-under partner work. These sequences do not replace the dialogue; they abstracted the emotion that dialogue cannot fully express.

In structural terms, these movement passages function like the heightened soliloquies in classical drama: they signal that the play is stepping outside its naturalistic register to allow the audience to feel rather than analyse. As a performer, you must understand where you are in the seasonal structure when one of these sequences begins — the physical demands of a spring chair duet carry a different emotional charge from a winter one.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly movement sequences interrupt the naturalistic dialogue at moments of heightened emotion. They are structural devices, not decoration: they show what characters feel but cannot say.

The Shock Ending: Dramatic Irony in Retrospect

Bovell builds a late-play revelation about Bob — a revelation that casts new light on everything that has preceded it. This is a structural device Bovell uses across his work: the thing you think you know is retrospectively undone. The audience carries their understanding of Bob through all four seasons and then, in winter, discovers they have been watching with incomplete information.

For a director, the challenge is to stage the ending so that the tableau at the play's close resonates with every earlier tableau the audience has seen. The ending must feel both surprising and, in retrospect, inevitable — the hallmark of precisely engineered dramatic structure. In production, designers often use a sudden, stark shift in the lighting state to mark the revelation: a wash that was warm and amber throughout the summer season becomes a cold, bare white or a near-blackout, so that the structural shock is felt as a physical change in the space.

Students sometimes treat the direct-address passages as straightforward narration — information delivery. In fact, they are structurally complex. Rosie's monologues are spoken from a temporal perspective that is partly ahead of where the action has reached. This means the audience is in a state of partial dramatic irony: they sense that things will go wrong before they go wrong. As a performer playing Rosie, the challenge is to hold both timeframes in your body: the innocence of the present tense and the knowledge of the future. Physically, this might mean a stillness that contrasts with the movement of the scenes around her, positioning her slightly apart — at upstage centre, separated from the family activity downstage — to suggest her dual temporal position.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
When analysing the play’s structure in practice, avoid simply retelling events. Explain how a structural choice shapes the audience’s response. Ask what the seasonal frame, the accumulation of revelations or a shift in theatrical register allows Bovell to communicate.

For an extended response, use the performer or designer perspective named in the question. Keep every choice specific, link it to a moment in the play and explain its intended effect on the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bovell structures the play around four seasons, each foregrounding one child's revelation, building cumulative emotional weight towards a late-play shock that re-orders what the audience believed.
  • The kitchen and the rose garden are twin centres: the garden is a recurring symbol of Bob's emotional life; proxemics between these spaces carries meaning for a director.
  • Frantic Assembly movement sequences are structural devices, not decoration: they mark the moments where naturalistic dialogue cannot hold the emotion, and a designer's lighting choices should reflect the seasonal arc throughout.

lessons.title: Characters: The Price Family
lessons.content_html:
The Price Family: Six Characters, Six Truths

At the centre of Things I Know to Be True are six characters whose individual arcs intersect and collide across one year. Bovell constructs each character through a combination of naturalistic characterisation and carefully placed revelation. None of the six is a simple figure. The parents have their own secrets; the children's crises are not resolved neatly. Understanding each character's motivation is essential for answering performer-focused questions and for analysing how Bovell stages the tensions between them.

Bob Price — The Father

Bob is a retired man whose identity is bound up in the rose garden. He is quietly principled and emotionally guarded: a man who loves his family but finds direct emotional expression difficult. On stage, Bob's relationship with the garden anchors his proxemics: when he is in the garden alone, he is at his most settled. When a child intrudes into that space, his physical stillness — a characteristic upright posture, hands engaged with the plants — can shift to a sudden tension in the shoulders, a hesitation before he turns. As a performer playing Bob, you would use a slower pace and lower vocal register to convey his measured, restrained quality, contrasting sharply with the moments when emotion breaks through his composure.

Bob carries a secret that is not fully revealed until winter. A performer must therefore play Bob with a layer of contained guilt or private knowledge beneath the surface of his public manner, without signalling the secret prematurely. This is classic Stanislavskian work: knowing the character's given circumstances in full, even when the audience does not yet know them.

Key Fact

Bob is emotionally guarded and principled, defined by his attachment to the rose garden. A performer must carry the weight of a concealed revelation while sustaining the surface of a loving but reserved father.

Fran Price — The Mother

Fran is a nurse: direct-spoken, pragmatic and tougher than Bob in her immediate emotional responses. She is the domestic authority of the kitchen, and Bovell frequently stages her interactions with the children in that space, where her command is physical and verbal. As a performer, Fran requires a brisk, purposeful quality: a precise, clipped delivery that can suddenly crack when she is confronted with something she is not prepared for. The contrast between her professional competence — a nurse who handles crisis daily — and her shock at her children's revelations is a key dramatic irony that a performer can exploit.

In staging terms, a lighting designer might use a warmer, directed lighting special on Fran in kitchen scenes to reinforce her as the emotional centre of this domestic space, contrasting with the more diffuse exterior quality of the garden lighting.

The Four Children

Each child is given a distinct arc and a contrasting relationship to their parents' expectations. Pip, the eldest, is leaving her marriage and her city; her revelation is about her own agency and the cost of self-determination. Her scenes with Fran carry the deepest confrontation between the women: the mother who stayed and the daughter who is leaving. A performer playing Pip must convey both the guilt of abandonment and the urgency of self-liberation — often simultaneously, in a single scene.

Mark undergoes gender transition and returns as Mia. Bovell treats this arc with careful dramatic attention. The script charts the journey across the summer season, showing how each member of the family responds differently to a transformation they may not have expected. As a performer, the challenge is to play Mark's revelation with specificity: the particular mixture of vulnerability and assertion that comes from speaking a truth about yourself to people whose acceptance matters most. Physically, the movement sequences around this arc can carry a quality of both constraint and release, as Frantic Assembly's contact work is used to express what the dialogue cannot.

Ben, the corporate financier, has been embezzling. His autumn revelation is marked by a different register: the shame of exposure in a family that values hard work and honesty. Ben's scenes with Bob carry the burden of a son seeking his father's judgement. A performer might use a tightly controlled stillness that gradually deteriorates — a tightening of the jaw, a slower and more effortful pace of speech — as the confession progresses.

Rosie, the youngest daughter, returns from Berlin heartbroken. She is the play's narrator-figure: the character who speaks directly to the audience and who appears to hold knowledge the other characters do not. Her performer–audience relationship is more openly mediated than the others'. In staging, Rosie is often placed at upstage centre or slightly apart from the family groupings when she addresses the audience, so that her dual role — participant in the family drama and witness to it — is visible in the blocking.

Character questions need concrete vocal and physical specificity. For the Mark / Mia arc, a strong answer avoids generalising and instead describes distinct physical and vocal choices for distinct moments. For example: in the scene where Mark speaks to the parents, a performer might use a measured vocal pace with deliberate pauses, a sustained level gaze at each parent in turn rather than looking away, and an open but grounded posture — weight through both feet, hands relaxed — to communicate both the vulnerability of the moment and the assertion of self-knowledge. This is very different from the physicality of Ben's shame-filled confession, which calls for more restricted, self-protective gestures.

The proxemic distance between Mark and each parent at this moment is itself a staging decision: how close does Bob stand? Does Fran move towards her child or remain behind the kitchen counter? These choices communicate the parents' responses before any dialogue is spoken.

Key Fact

The six Price family members each require distinct vocal and physical characterisation. Bovell builds contrast into the family's dynamics: Bob (restrained, guarded), Fran (direct, purposeful), Pip (urgent, guilty), Mark (vulnerable yet assertive), Ben (controlled, deteriorating), Rosie (narrator-witness).

Students sometimes treat Bob and Fran as a single parental bloc — two people who respond identically to their children's revelations. Bovell does not write them that way. They have different emotional registers, different relationships with each child, and, crucially, different secrets. In staging, a director might use the physical geography of the kitchen and garden to reinforce this: Fran rarely enters the garden (her territory is the kitchen), so when she does cross into Bob's space, the proxemics of that crossing signals a shift in the power dynamic between them.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For the 8-mark performer question, the most common error is describing what the character is feeling without translating it into specific vocal and physical choices at a named moment. “I would act nervously” earns no marks. Instead: “As a performer playing Ben in the confession scene with Bob, I would use a slower pace of speech, dropping my volume to near-whisper, while physically turning slightly away from Bob — a three-quarter profile that suggests both the wish to speak and the instinct to withdraw.” Every performer answer needs a named moment, a specific vocal quality and a specific physical choice.

For the 20-mark extended staging response, the question may focus on a specific character interaction. Use the kitchen / garden geography to anchor your design choices: lighting can distinguish the two spaces, costume can signal character status and register, and the proxemics between characters in a given scene are the director's most powerful vocabulary for communicating family dynamics.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each of the six Price family members requires distinct vocal and physical characterisation: Bob is guarded and principled; Fran is direct and purposeful; each child is defined by the nature of their revelation and their relationship to parental expectation.
  • Mark / Mia's arc demands performer specificity at each moment of the journey; credit goes to concrete vocal and physical choices anchored to the specific point in the arc, not generalised sentiment.
  • The kitchen / garden geography gives a director a powerful proxemics language: which characters enter which space, and when, communicates shifts in power and emotional alignment before a word is spoken.

Every choice is justified with a named effect on the audience.

lessons.title: Themes: Family, Identity, Truth
lessons.content_html:
What the Play Asks Us to Believe

Things I Know to Be True draws its title from a phrase that challenges certainty. The things we know to be true about our families — their loyalty, their stability, their love — are exactly what the play systematically tests. Andrew Bovell structures the play's themes around the tension between what the Price family projects outwardly (a settled suburban life, parental pride, sibling solidarity) and what is actually concealed beneath that surface. For a dramatist, this gap between appearance and reality is a rich seam of dramatic irony.

Family: Conditional and Unconditional Love

The dominant theme of the play is family itself: what it can absorb, what it cannot, and who pays the cost of loyalty. Bovell explores two competing models of parental love through Bob and Fran. Fran's love is fierce and vocal; Bob's is quieter and harder to read. The play tests whether parental love is truly unconditional — offered regardless of what a child does or who they are — or whether it carries conditions that only a revelation can expose.

In staging this theme, a director working with the proxemics of the family group can communicate volumes before dialogue begins. When all six characters occupy the stage together, the distances between them — who stands near whom, who gravitates towards a parent, who is physically at the margin of the group — form an instant visual map of the family's emotional geography. A production using a proscenium arch configuration might arrange the family in a tableau that places Bob and Fran at the apex, with the four children arranged at varying distances, so that the staging enacts the theme of parental expectation as a gravitational force.

Key Fact

The central question of the play is whether the family's love is truly unconditional. Each of the four children's revelations tests this question from a different direction: departure, identity, criminality and grief.

Identity: Gender, Self-Determination and the Family's Gaze

The theme of identity runs through every character arc. For Mark, identity is the most explicit subject: the summer season stages the journey of a character coming forward with a truth about who they are in gender terms. Bovell handles this arc with dramatic care, showing the parents' different responses and the sibling dynamics around the revelation. For a performer, the challenge is to play the specific mixture of assertion and vulnerability that characterises a moment of authentic self-disclosure.

Frantic Assembly's movement sequences are structurally significant here. Contact improvisation and the round-by-through-under vocabulary can express the bodily dimension of identity — the sense of inhabiting a self more fully — in a way that pure dialogue cannot. A designer working on this section of the play might use cross-fading between lighting states to mark the transition between the family's before-and-after relationship with Mark / Mia, rather than a single sudden shift.

For Pip, identity is about self-determination: leaving a marriage and a city is an act of individual will that the family reads as abandonment. For Rosie, identity is the most existential: she is the character who must find meaning after heartbreak and who speaks from the play's narrative edge. Identity is also a theme for the parents themselves: Bob's late-revealed secret reframes who he is in the audience's understanding, retroactively altering the identity they believed they had witnessed across the whole play.

This arc needs to be treated with specificity and respect for the character. Vague generalisations or language that editorialises about the subject matter earn no credit. Strong answers describe what a performer or director actually does on stage: specific vocal choices, specific physical choices, specific lighting and costume decisions that serve the character's journey at each stage of the arc.

A lighting designer might use a warm but precise lighting special on Mark / Mia during the revelation scene, isolating them from the family group while the family is lit in a broader, cooler wash. This separation in the lighting state communicates the character's position: fully present with the family yet briefly occupying a different emotional space. As Mia is accepted back into the family warmth, the isolated special can gradually fade into the shared wash, a visual enactment of inclusion.

Truth, Secrets and the Things We Don't Know

Alongside the children's revelations, the play harbours two parental secrets: Bob's concealed infidelity and the late-play shock that reframes his character. These secrets introduce the theme of truth itself as a complex, unstable thing. What the family has built together — their shared history, their mutual understanding — turns out to rest on partial information. Bovell suggests that all families are, to some degree, fictions that each member maintains for the others.

The rose garden carries this theme in physical form. A prop as symbol, the roses represent the beauty Bob cultivates and the concealment required to maintain it: a garden needs tending, work, constant management, just as a long marriage does. As a set designer, using the garden's seasonal change — spring blossom, summer fullness, autumn decay, bare winter stems — to mirror the play's structural arc makes the theme of concealed truth visible across the whole production.

Money, Ageing and Australian Suburbia

Ben's arc introduces the theme of financial wrongdoing and the gap between a child's projected success and their private reality. The theme here is the pressure of family expectation: the child who is supposed to have succeeded and has not. A performer playing Ben must communicate the layered quality of this shame — personal guilt, dread of a father's disappointment, awareness that his crime will affect the whole family.

Bovell also explores the theme of ageing parents and the moment when adult children see their parents as fallible. The Price parents are settled into late middle age when the play begins; by its end, they are irrevocably changed. The Australian suburban setting — a comfortable home, a tended garden, the domestic certainties of middle-class life in contemporary Adelaide — provides the context against which every destabilising revelation lands. The ordinariness of the setting is the point: the play insists that its themes are universal.

Students sometimes treat the play's themes as separate compartments — one child's arc = one theme. Bovell's work is more integrated than this. Identity runs through every character, not just Mark / Mia. Truth and concealment are as relevant to Bob's infidelity as to Ben's embezzlement. Family love is tested by Pip's departure just as much as by Ben's arrest. Strong exam answers draw thematic connections across the play rather than treating each season in isolation.

Key Fact

The rose garden embodies the play's central theme: the beauty that is cultivated outwardly and the concealment that sustains it. Designing the garden to change across the four seasons makes the theme of truth and hidden lives visible throughout the production.

For an extended response, use the performer or designer perspective named in the question. Give detailed choices relevant to that role, link them to the extract and the whole play, and explain their intended effects.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play's central theme is the tension between outward family stability and concealed individual truth: each revelation tests whether the Price family's love is conditional or unconditional.
  • Identity runs through every character arc, not just Mark / Mia's; the theme of truth and concealment connects Bob's infidelity, Ben's embezzlement and Pip's departure.
  • The rose garden is a prop-as-symbol that carries the theme of concealment across the whole production; a designer who changes the garden across the four seasons makes the play's thematic arc visible.

lessons.title: Context: Bovell, Frantic Assembly and 2016 Adelaide
lessons.content_html:
Andrew Bovell: Playwright of Family Secrets

Andrew Bovell was born in 1962 in Australia. He is one of the most significant Australian playwrights of his generation, working across theatre and screen. His theatre writing is characterised by an interest in family, secrets, and the long shadow of the past on the present. His play Speaking in Tongues (1996) was adapted into the acclaimed film Lantana. His When the Rain Stops Falling (2008) traces a family across four generations and two continents, exploring the way inherited secrets reverberate through time.

Understanding Bovell's broader work helps explain his approach to Things I Know to Be True. He is not a playwright interested in simple moral resolution. His families are flawed, his parents are fallible, and his plays typically end with a revelation that refuses to tidy itself away. In staging terms, this means a designer must plan for a production that does not deliver comfort: the lighting state at the end of a Bovell play is more likely to strip the stage bare than to bathe it in warmth.

Key Fact

Andrew Bovell (born 1962, Australia) is known for plays about family secrets and inherited trauma. When the Rain Stops Falling (2008) and Speaking in Tongues (1996) are his other major theatre works. The AQA set play is published in the Nick Hern Modern Plays edition.

Frantic Assembly: Physical Theatre as Structural Language

Physical theatre is a performance mode in which the body carries meaning as centrally as spoken language. Frantic Assembly, the British company co-founded by Scott Graham and Steven Hoggett in 1994, is one of the defining physical theatre companies of their generation. Their method of building productions blends text with devised movement, and their signature vocabulary includes chair duets, partner lifts, round-by-through-under sequences and contact improvisation work.

What makes Things I Know to Be True distinctive in the AQA set play list is that it was co-developed with Frantic Assembly. Bovell and Scott Graham worked on the play together: the movement sequences are not choreographed additions to a finished text but are built into the play's structure at the writing stage. The stage directions specify where these sequences occur and broadly describe their physical quality. This integration means that Frantic Assembly's aesthetic is not decorative but structural: a production of the play that removed the movement sequences would be a different play.

For a student approaching the play as a designer or director, the Frantic Assembly context has direct practical implications. The movement sequences require a stage space that allows full-body contact work: a very cluttered set or a small thrust stage would limit their impact. A production on a wide proscenium arch stage can use the depth of the stage effectively, placing the movement sequences in a broader upstage space while naturalistic dialogue scenes play in a more intimate downstage area.

Bovell's approach to character sits firmly in the Stanislavskian tradition: the Price family members are psychologically specific, driven by clearly articulated objectives and given circumstances. Their naturalistic dialogue scenes demand the kind of truthful, interior-driven performance that Stanislavski's system develops.

Frantic Assembly's movement sequences, however, operate in a different register. They are not naturalistic: a character does not lift their sibling in a stylised arc because that is what people literally do when they argue. The movement abstracts the emotional truth. The hybrid form of the play — Stanislavskian naturalism interrupted by Frantic Assembly physicality — means that performers must be trained in both modes and must be able to shift between them convincingly within a single scene. This is a significant practical demand and a rich source of exam questions about practitioner application.

Adelaide, 2016: The Contemporary Australian Setting

The play is set in contemporary Adelaide, South Australia. Adelaide is a city often associated in Australian cultural imagination with suburban respectability, middle-class aspiration and a certain quiet conservatism — a city where people know what is expected of them. Bovell uses this context to make the Price family's story both specific (Australian, contemporary, suburban) and universal (family secrets, generational conflict, the distance between who we are and who others expect us to be).

The play premiered at the State Theatre Company South Australia in May 2016, the first performance in Adelaide. It then transferred later that year to the UK in a Frantic Assembly co-production at the Lyric Hammersmith in London, directed by Geordie Brookman and Scott Graham, followed by a UK tour. The British audience encountered the play as both a foreign text (Australian voices, Australian suburban landscape) and a recognisable one: the themes of family, identity and parental love cross cultural contexts. For an exam answer about context, this dual reception is significant: Bovell writes from inside Australian suburbia but with full awareness that the play will be received internationally.

Key Fact

World premiere: State Theatre Company South Australia, Adelaide, May 2016. UK premiere: Lyric Hammersmith / Frantic Assembly co-production, 2016, directed by Geordie Brookman and Scott Graham. The play sits within Australian suburban-realist theatre but is shaped by British physical theatre practice.

Context in the Design Room: What 2016 Adelaide Means Practically

Context shapes design choices. A production setting the play in its original Adelaide context might use warm, sun-bleached costume colours for the parents — indicating outdoor suburban life — while giving the returning children clothes that suggest their distance from home (Rosie in Berlin-influenced layering, Ben in corporate wear that reads as slightly out of place in the back garden). The costume design can communicate, without a word, where each character has come from and how far they have travelled from their parents' world.

The garden itself, in design terms, is the single most important set element for communicating context. A designer using real or artificial rose plants, a warm earth-coloured floor cloth, and a kitchen visible behind a glass or gauze partition is immediately communicating Australian suburban domesticity. Lighting in this setting tends towards warm ambers in the garden during daytime scenes and cooler, more interior tones in the kitchen — a lighting wash that shifts in quality between the two spaces to reinforce their symbolic difference.

Students sometimes treat the movement sequences as an interesting add-on to an otherwise straight naturalistic play. This fundamentally misunderstands the co-development process. Bovell and Graham built the movement sequences into the structure of the play: they occur at moments where the emotional content exceeds what naturalistic dialogue can carry. Removing them would remove some of the play's most significant meaning-making moments. In any answer about the play's form and style, students should describe it as a hybrid form: naturalistic family drama with integrated physical theatre sequences, rather than naturalism with optional dance interludes.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Andrew Bovell (born 1962) is an Australian playwright whose work consistently explores family secrets and the destabilising effect of revealed truth; the Nick Hern Modern Plays edition is the prescribed text for AQA.
  • Frantic Assembly co-developed the play with Bovell: the movement sequences are structural, not decorative, and require performers trained in both Stanislavskian naturalism and physical theatre.
  • The contemporary Adelaide setting gives designers a specific visual and cultural language (suburban warmth, garden, domestic kitchen) and makes the play's themes both locally specific and internationally universal.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Monologue and Movement
lessons.content_html:
Two Languages in One Play

Andrew Bovell gives Things I Know to Be True two distinct theatrical languages that work in counterpoint throughout the play. The first is naturalistic family dialogue — the everyday speech of a suburban household, full of interruptions, silences and unfinished thoughts. The second is a more openly theatrical language: direct address monologue and stylised physical movement. Understanding how Bovell moves between these two registers — and what that movement achieves for the audience — is central to answering any question about dramatic methods in this play.

The alternation is structural. Naturalistic scenes establish the domestic reality of the Price family: their relationships, their habits, the particular tensions of a household where four adult children are still emotionally tied to parents who are themselves imperfect. Then, at moments of heightened emotion, the register shifts. A character steps outside the scene to speak directly to the audience, or the family moves into a Frantic Assembly movement sequence that says in bodies what cannot be said in words.

Key Fact

Bovell uses two theatrical registers: naturalistic dialogue (characters speak to each other as real people might) and direct address (a character speaks directly to the audience, stepping outside the scene). Moving between these registers is itself a dramatic method.

Rosie and the Art of Direct Address

Rosie functions as the play’s primary narrator-figure. Her monologue passages are spoken from a temporal position that is partly outside the action: she often knows, or half-knows, what the season will bring. This creates a layer of dramatic irony — the audience senses things will go wrong before they do, sharing a partial foreknowledge with Rosie that the other characters do not have.

In production, the staging of Rosie’s direct-address passages must communicate her dual temporal position. A director might place her at upstage centre while the family activity continues downstage, visually separating her narrator-self from her character-self. A lighting designer might use a tight lighting special to pull her out of the general lighting wash, signalling to the audience that she is speaking from a different register of truth.

Students sometimes treat Rosie’s direct-address passages as straightforward narration — a way of telling the audience what is happening. This misreads their function. Rosie’s monologues carry subtext: they express what she feels but cannot say to the family, and they position the audience as her confidant rather than a detached observer. As a performer playing Rosie, you are not reporting; you are sharing something that costs you emotionally. The vocal and physical choices must reflect that emotional cost. Speaking at a steady, measured pace with a slightly lower volume than the dialogue scenes suggests intimacy; allowing brief pauses before key revelations gives the audience space to feel the weight of what is coming.

Movement as Subtext: The Frantic Assembly Sequences

The physical theatre sequences in Things I Know to Be True were developed in collaboration with Frantic Assembly, the British physical theatre company co-directed by Scott Graham. Frantic Assembly’s approach to movement is rooted in everyday physicality rather than stylised dance: they build sequences from contact improvisation, counter-balance, and the reordering of familiar gestures. The result is movement that feels emotionally urgent rather than aesthetically decorative.

In this play, the movement sequences function as heightened subtext. When the Price family’s emotional life exceeds what their naturalistic dialogue can hold, Bovell’s stage directions call for a physical sequence. These moments might involve a lift that expresses both love and the effort of holding a relationship together, a chair duet that externalises a conversation neither character can have in words, or the round-by-through-under contact work in which bodies pass through each other’s space, suggesting emotional entanglement.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly movement sequences in the play externalise subtext: the things characters feel but cannot verbalise. A lift might express the effort of parental love; a chair duet might show the negotiation inside a relationship. The movement is not illustrative — it reveals.

The Garden Monologue and Rose Imagery

Bob’s rose garden is not simply a set piece; it is a recurring motif that carries a great deal of the play’s emotional weight without being stated directly. When Bob speaks in or near the garden — tending, pruning, simply being — the garden becomes the physical correlative of his inner life: ordered, carefully maintained, beautiful in a way that the rest of his world is not. In staging terms, a sound designer might build a subtle soundscape for the garden: birdsong, a light breeze, the distant sound of cicadas in summer — sounds that contrast with the harder, closer acoustic of the kitchen interior.

The rose imagery also works in conjunction with mood and atmosphere. In spring, the roses are beginning: fresh colour, the optimism of new growth. By winter, bare stems. A designer who makes the rose bush a visible element of the set can track this seasonal arc visually, so that the garden itself becomes a kind of scenic narrator — telling the audience where in the emotional year they are without any dialogue needing to do that work.

As a performer delivering a direct-address monologue, you face a specific challenge: you are speaking to the audience, not to another character, so the usual triggers of reaction and response are removed. To hold this, you must anchor each moment in a specific thought or feeling. Vocally, you might use a slower pace than the dialogue scenes, a slightly raised head so that eye-line reaches out across the auditorium, and variation in volume — dropping to near-quiet for the most privately held thoughts. Physically, stillness is a powerful choice: if the rest of the production is in motion, a still figure speaking directly out commands attention.

As a lighting designer, a direct-address monologue offers the chance to make a distinct visual statement. Removing the character from the general wash and placing them in a tight profile spot — a warm amber or a cooler neutral depending on the season — signals the change in register without any spoken announcement. If the family remains dimly visible upstage in a reduced wash while Rosie speaks downstage in a special, the audience holds two simultaneous spaces: the world of the family and the world of the narrator. This dual focus is one of the most effective staging solutions for the monologue moments.
lessons.exam_tip_html:

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bovell writes in two theatrical registers: naturalistic dialogue and direct-address monologue / stylised movement. The shift between them is itself a dramatic method, signalling to the audience that the play is moving into a different kind of truth.
  • Rosie’s direct-address monologues create dramatic irony: she speaks from partial foreknowledge, making the audience share a sense of what is coming before it arrives. As a performer, this demands holding two timeframes in the body simultaneously.
  • Frantic Assembly movement sequences externalise subtext — the emotional content that dialogue cannot contain. The rose garden’s soundscape and lighting state can reinforce the seasonal arc, giving the play a visual and auditory narrative that runs in parallel to the spoken one.

lessons.title: Staging and Design: The Garden and the Kitchen
lessons.content_html:
Two Spaces, One Stage

The staging challenge at the heart of Things I Know to Be True is how to hold two fundamentally different spaces on stage simultaneously: the suburban kitchen, Fran’s practical domestic territory, and the rose garden, Bob’s emotional refuge. Both spaces must feel inhabited throughout the play; characters move between them, and that movement is always meaningful. A set design solution for this play must therefore do two things at once: establish the domestic realism of a contemporary Australian home and signal, through the choice of materials, levels and visual contrast, that the garden carries a weight beyond the literal.

Many production approaches use a largely bare stage with carefully chosen scenic elements: a kitchen table and chairs upstage to one side, a patch of soil or a single rose bush to the other. The simplicity prevents the design from competing with the play’s emotional register. The audience is asked to invest imaginatively in the spaces, and they will do so provided the key scenic signatures are clear: the hardness of the kitchen floor against the softness of the garden earth, the enclosed quality of the interior against the open expanse of the outdoor space.

Key Fact

The kitchen and the rose garden are the play’s twin centres. A designer’s task is to make them coexist on a shared stage while keeping their distinct qualities clear: the kitchen is practical and enclosed; the garden is open, symbolic and emotionally loaded.

Lighting the Seasons

Because the play moves through a full year in four seasons, a lighting designer has an unusually rich palette to work with. The seasonal arc creates a ready-made visual narrative: the lighting should track the emotional temperature of the play as much as the literal time of day. In spring, a warm, hopeful lighting state makes sense — perhaps a yellow-gold wash from a front-of-house wash bar, suggesting the optimism of new beginnings. By winter, the same space should feel colder and more exposed: a shift to a bluer, flatter wash, with reduced intensity, creates the emotional chill of the play’s ending without needing any text to announce it.

The garden, as an outdoor space, invites naturalistic lighting choices. Australian summer light is bright, high and unforgiving: a strong overhead source, perhaps a single profile lantern at steep angle to suggest midday sun, combined with a warm Fresnel fill from the side, would give the summer garden its harsh brightness. When the play moves into autumn and winter, the overhead angle softens; the fills are withdrawn. The physical sense of light shrinking is inseparable from the emotional sense of the family’s certainties contracting.

A gobo is one of the most versatile tools available to a lighting designer who needs to suggest organic, natural spaces on an otherwise bare stage. A leaf-break or branch-pattern gobo projected across the garden area would dapple the ground and the performers with shifting light and shadow, suggesting the presence of trees or foliage without any physical set element needing to represent it. In the spring and summer garden scenes, this gobo might be used with a warm amber gel; by autumn, the same gobo with an orange-red gel creates the impression of dying leaves. By winter, the gobo is withdrawn entirely: bare, flat light for a bare garden. The gobo therefore participates in the seasonal arc of the whole design.

Sound Design: Cicadas, Birdsong and the Kitchen Underscore

Sound design in this play must distinguish between two acoustic environments: the inside of the kitchen and the outside of the garden. This distinction is not just about realism; it is about the play’s emotional grammar. The kitchen is the space of direct confrontation — Fran’s world, where practical truths are spoken. The garden is the space of private feeling and slower time. A sound designer who understands this will create two distinct sonic environments and manage the transition between them carefully.

For the garden, a soundscape of cicadas and birdsong establishes the Australian summer setting while also carrying an emotional quality: the warmth and continuity of the natural world contrasting with the disruptions the children bring. As the seasons turn, the soundscape changes: autumn might bring a wind underscore, winter a near-silence broken only by rain. For the kitchen scenes, the sound design can afford to be more minimal — perhaps a low, barely perceptible underscore in the most emotionally charged confrontations, or simply the ambient sounds of a domestic interior: the distant hum of a refrigerator, the sound of water from a tap. These diegetic sounds ground the audience in the domestic reality of the space.

Key Fact

The sound design must create two distinct acoustic environments. The garden: a seasonal soundscape (cicadas in summer, wind in autumn, near-silence in winter). The kitchen: minimal underscore or diegetic domestic sounds. The shift between these environments should be part of every transition between the two spaces.

Costume Design: Season and Character

Costume in this play operates primarily in a naturalistic register: the Price family are a contemporary suburban Australian family, and their clothing should reflect that. Jeans, casual shirts, the particular textures of modern working life. However, the seasonal structure gives a costume designer the opportunity to make the passage of time visible through clothing. Pip’s spring arrival might be in light layers — linen or cotton in pale colours suggesting something new and tentative. Mark’s summer scenes might carry the heat of the season in warmer fabrics and colours. By winter, the clothing grows heavier, more protective.

The more significant costume choice concerns Mark’s arc as he transitions to Mia. The play tracks this across the summer season. A costume designer must collaborate closely with the director and, above all, with the performer to make choices that are specific, respectful and character-driven rather than generalised. Early in the summer season, Mark’s clothing might reflect a tentative, not yet fully expressed identity. As the season reaches its peak — the moment of revelation with his parents — costume choices can carry the weight of that honesty: a clarity and simplicity of dress that signals that a decision has been made. The silhouette matters: a costume that fits the body honestly communicates something very different from one that is performing concealment.

Imagine a scene in the winter garden in which Bob tends the rose bush alone before Rosie arrives to speak with him. As a lighting designer, you would begin with the winter state established earlier: a cold, blue-white wash from a single overhead Fresnel, shadows long and hard, the gobo withdrawn so that only bare, flat light reaches the stage. The rose bush itself — a physical set element, bare-stemmed in winter — is lit separately by a downstage floor birdies unit with a pale amber gel, so that it glows slightly warmer than the space around it: still alive, still present. Bob is in the garden’s main wash. When Rosie enters from the kitchen side, the kitchen’s interior warm light briefly spills into the garden area before the door closes: a cross-fade that registers her arrival as a change in the light. As a sound designer, you would fade the winter soundscape (a low wind underscore, near-silence) to near-nothing as their conversation begins, so that the words land in absolute acoustic clarity. As a costume designer, Bob wears a heavier, darker jacket — navy or charcoal — and Rosie’s winter coat in a contrasting lighter fabric: they are the same family, but the visual contrast of their costumes keeps them subtly individualised. Every design choice in this moment supports the emotional content: the coldness of the season, the fragility of the rose, the weight of what has not yet been said.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
When developing a design response, avoid general descriptions such as “dark lighting to create a sad mood”. Name the design elements, describe how they would be used at a specific moment and explain the effect on the audience.

For a 20-mark design response, develop detailed choices in the one design specialism named in the question. Link them to the extract and the whole play, and explain their intended effect on the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The kitchen and the garden must coexist on a shared stage with clearly distinct qualities: the kitchen is practical and enclosed; the garden is open, symbolic and emotionally loaded. Set, lighting and sound all play a role in maintaining this distinction.
  • The seasonal arc (spring to winter) gives the lighting designer a structural palette: warm, high and bright in spring and summer; colder, flatter and more stripped by autumn and winter. A gobo can track this arc without any physical scene change.
  • Sound design uses two distinct environments: a seasonal soundscape for the garden (cicadas, wind, near-silence) and a minimal or diegetic domestic acoustic for the kitchen. Costume reflects both naturalistic character and the seasonal passage of time, with Mark’s arc demanding particular sensitivity and specificity.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Bob's Final Tableau
lessons.content_html:
Performing a Family Under Pressure

The Price family in Things I Know to Be True are ordinary people in an extraordinary year. Each character carries a different kind of pressure, and a performer’s job is to hold that pressure truthfully across the entire arc of the play — not only in the big revelatory scenes but in the domestic moments in between. Andrew Bovell’s naturalistic dialogue gives performers rich material: overlapping thoughts, sentences that stop before they finish, the particular shorthand of a family that has been talking to each other for decades. Understanding how to use vocal interpretation and physical interpretation for each character is the foundation of every performance answer in the exam.

This lesson focuses on Bob, Fran, and the four children at the play’s most charged moments: Bob’s stoicism in the face of his children’s revelations; Fran’s directness and toughness; Mark’s reveal scene; Pip’s departure; and the ensemble physicality of the play’s ending tableau. In each case, the performer must balance what the character says with what the character cannot say — the subtext that Bovell builds into every scene.

Key Fact

For every performance question, you must name both vocal AND physical choices, anchored to a specific named moment. Saying “I would act sad” is not enough. Name the tool: slower pace, a drop in volume, a held pause; or a stillness in the body, a lowered gaze, hands released to the sides. The more specific you are, the higher the mark.

Bob: Stoicism and the Weight of What Is Unsaid

Bob Price is a study in restraint. He tends his roses, maintains a sense of order, and responds to each of his children’s revelations with a quietness that the audience must learn to read. His silence is not emptiness; it is full of suppressed feeling. A performer playing Bob must understand this as the central technical challenge of the role: how to communicate emotional depth through stillness and economy rather than through display.

In the garden scenes, Bob’s physicality can be rooted in a specific task — he is pruning, or turning soil, or standing with his hands at his sides among the plants. Proxemics matter enormously for this character: when a child approaches him in the garden, the way Bob adjusts his position — whether he turns fully to face them, or continues his task with his body angled slightly away, or holds himself very still — communicates volumes before a word is spoken. Vocally, Bob speaks measured, unhurried. A slower pace than the other characters; pauses before significant responses; a volume that does not rise even under pressure. When he receives a revelation that shocks him, the most powerful choice is often to lower the volume still further: a near-whisper that forces the audience to lean in.

The winter scene in which Mark tells his parents that he is transitioning to Mia is one of the play’s most complex performance challenges. For the performer playing Mark, the approach must be grounded in the character’s specific circumstances: this is not a generalised coming-out scene but a particular person, in a particular family, telling two particular parents something that has cost him an enormous amount to hold back. The given circumstances — who Bob is, who Fran is, how the family communicates — shape every choice.

Vocally, the performer playing Mark might begin the scene with a pace that is slightly faster than usual — the energy of something that must be said before the courage runs out — and then slow significantly once the words are out, allowing the silence of the parents’ response to land. Physically, Mark might begin the scene at a measured distance from his parents — neither close nor far, a neutral proxemics — and during the most difficult part of the speech take a step towards them rather than away, communicating that the revelation is an act of trust rather than an exit. A small, specific gesture — the hands open, facing upward, at the sides, as if offering something — can communicate vulnerability without overplaying the emotional register. Specificity is what counts: not “I would look scared” but “I would hold my body very still from the waist down while allowing a slight tremor in the hands, so that the effort of physical control is visible to the audience.”

Fran: Directness Under Pressure

Where Bob retreats into stillness, Fran advances. She is the more direct of the two parents — a nurse by profession, accustomed to saying difficult things plainly. A performer playing Fran must resist the temptation to play her as simply hard. Her directness is a form of love: she speaks truth because she believes her children deserve it. The challenge is to hold both qualities in the body at once: the toughness and the vulnerability beneath it.

In the kitchen confrontation scenes, Fran’s physicality is active: she might be at the kitchen counter or the table, engaged in a practical task, and she continues that task for longer than is comfortable while a conversation is beginning around her. This use of physical business — the act of doing something with the hands while a difficult emotional conversation unfolds — is a classic Stanislavskian approach to grounding a scene in physical reality. When Fran finally stops and turns to face the person she is speaking with, the stillness of that turn communicates that something significant is now happening.

Key Fact

Fran’s directness is grounded in physical business: she works with her hands while conversations unfold around her, and the moment she stops signals to the audience that something real is now being said. As a performer, using and then releasing physical business is a precise technique for controlling the rhythm of a scene.

The Ensemble and the Ending Tableau

The play’s final image is a tableau — the whole family gathered in a configuration that carries the weight of everything the year has delivered. In the Frantic Assembly co-production tradition, this moment may be embedded within or arrived at through a movement sequence: the family assembling themselves physically, finding their spatial relationship to each other and to Bob at the centre, so that the final image is not simply “they stand together” but a precisely constructed statement about love, damage, truth and endurance.

As a director working with the ensemble for this moment, the key decisions are about blocking and spatial hierarchy. Who is closest to Bob? Who is furthest away? Who makes physical contact with another character, and who is isolated? Does the tableau face the audience directly, or is it angled so that some characters have their backs to us, creating a sense of privacy or enclosure? Each of these decisions changes the meaning of the final image and must be justified in relation to the revelations the play has delivered across the year. The lighting state for the final tableau should be considered: a slow fade rather than a blackout, perhaps, so that the audience holds the image for longer — both literally and emotionally.

A common exam error in performance-interpretation answers is to describe what the character is feeling (“I would show that Bob is devastated”) rather than describing the specific vocal and physical choices that communicate that feeling without naming it. Audiences do not need to be told what a character feels; they need to be shown it through concrete theatrical means. Think of this as the difference between illustrating an emotion and communicating a thought. The character is not “performing sadness”; the character is pursuing a specific action (trying to hold themselves together, trying not to let a child see the damage their words have done), and it is that pursuit — the effort of it — that the audience reads as feeling. Always ask: what is this character doing, physically and vocally, in this moment? Start there, not with the emotion label.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For the 8-mark ‘Interpret as Performer’ question, you must give both a vocal AND a physical choice, each anchored to a named moment of the play. A common error is to write only about how the character feels without specifying the vocal or physical technique that communicates that feeling. The mark scheme requires: a specific vocal choice (e.g. “I would drop my volume to a near-whisper as Bob receives Mark’s news, slowing my pace to one beat per word so that each word lands separately”) AND a specific physical choice (e.g. “I would hold my body absolutely still, feet planted, hands released to my sides, allowing only the smallest shift of weight forward to communicate that I am listening with my whole self”). Name the moment, name the tools, explain the effect on the audience.

For a 20-mark response, use the performer or designer perspective named in the question. Keep your choices precise, link them to the extract and the whole play, and explain their intended effect on the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Every performance answer requires specific vocal AND physical choices anchored to a named moment. Naming the emotion is not enough; name the technique: volume, pace, pause, pitch; posture, gesture, proxemics, stillness.
  • Bob’s stoicism is communicated through restraint — a slower pace, near-whisper volume under pressure, stillness in the body; Fran’s directness through physical business that she then releases to signal importance. Both characters require technical precision rather than emotional display.
  • The ending tableau is an ensemble staging question: blocking, spatial hierarchy, physical contact, and the lighting state that holds the final image must all be considered together. The Frantic Assembly tradition of arriving at stillness through movement gives this moment particular theatrical weight.

Top band: Two or more specific vocal choices named and justified (e.g. a slowing of pace so that each subsequent word takes longer to arrive, signalling that Bob is processing; a drop in volume to near-whisper when he finally speaks, so the audience must work to hear him; a pause of three or four beats before his response, in which the silence itself is expressive). Upper-mid band: At least one named vocal and one named physical choice for the named moment; choices generally specific (not just 'I would speak quietly'); audience effect present. May not achieve the depth of Mastering but shows clear understanding of technique.

Lower-mid band: Relevant choices mentioned but described in general terms ('I would be quiet and still'); limited specificity; audience effect implied rather than explained.

Low band: Describes how Bob feels without naming specific vocal or physical techniques; no named moment; mostly descriptive.

Top band: Blocking and proxemics: specific positioning of named characters described and justified (e.g. Bob at centre, at floor level in the garden space, the four children arranged around him at measured distances that reflect their individual relationships to him — Rosie close, perhaps touching his arm; Mark/Mia at a slightly greater distance, standing tall and present; Ben further upstage, isolated; Pip equidistant). Physical contact specified (who touches whom, and why). Lower-mid band: Relevant staging ideas but general in execution; positions described without clear justification; lighting present but not specific; audience effect implied.

Low band: List of staging ideas without justification; one or two disciplines only; mostly descriptive.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Stanislavski Meets Frantic Assembly
lessons.content_html:
A Hybrid Form

Things I Know to Be True is one of very few GCSE set plays that is genuinely hybrid in its theatrical form: it was written to be performed using two distinct and historically separate performance traditions in the same production. The naturalistic family scenes draw on Stanislavskian acting principles. The movement sequences were developed in collaboration with Frantic Assembly and draw on physical theatre practice. Understanding both traditions and — crucially — how they interact in this play is the foundation of the practitioner-application question for this unit.

This is not a case of two traditions accidentally colliding. Bovell wrote the play specifically with Scott Graham of Frantic Assembly as a creative partner; the movement sequences are not added after the fact but are built into the dramatic structure. The result is a form where the transitions between registers — from dialogue to movement, from naturalism to physical abstraction — carry meaning in themselves. Understanding when and why those transitions happen is as important as understanding each tradition in isolation.

Key Fact

Things I Know to Be True uses two traditions deliberately: Stanislavskian emotional truth for the naturalistic dialogue scenes, and Frantic Assembly physical theatre for the movement sequences. Both are structural, not decorative. A student who treats the movement as ‘extra’ misses half the play’s theatrical language.

Stanislavski and the Price Family

Konstantin Stanislavski (1863–1938) developed a systematic approach to actor training that changed the way realistic drama is performed. His central insight was that truthful acting comes from the actor understanding the character’s inner life: their history, desires, relationships, and the specific circumstances of the scene. He called this the given circumstances. For a performer playing any member of the Price family, the given circumstances are richly specified by Bovell: each character’s profession, their history with each other, the year they are having, the specific weight they carry into each scene.

Stanislavski also asked actors to pursue an objective in every scene — a specific, playable goal that the character is trying to achieve. For Bob in the garden scenes, his objective might be simply “to keep this world intact” — to maintain the order and beauty of the space as a counterweight to the disorder his children keep introducing. For Fran in the kitchen confrontations, her objective might be “to make my child tell me the truth” or “to protect this family from what is coming.” When a performer anchors their choices to a clear objective, every physical and vocal decision becomes purposeful: it is always in the service of getting what the character wants.

For the performer playing Mark, whose arc moves towards his identity as Mia, Stanislavski’s given circumstances are particularly important. What lifts an answer is sensitive, specific choices that are grounded in who this character is in relation to this family. The given circumstances include: Mark’s relationship with his parents (the particular emotional dynamic of each parent); his sense of what the revelation will mean for the family; the specific setting (the kitchen or the garden, indoors or out, the season); and the circumstances that immediately precede the scene. A Stanislavskian performer does not play a generalised “coming out scene” — they play this character, in this moment, with these specific people. The choices that come from that specificity are always more compelling, and more mark-worthy, than the generic ones.

Frantic Assembly: Physical Theatre as Emotional Language

Frantic Assembly was founded in 1994 by Scott Graham, Steven Hoggett and Vicki Middleton. The company’s physical theatre practice is distinctive in that it is not primarily dance: it grows from everyday movement — the physicality of ordinary people — and heightens it into something expressive. Their key techniques include round-by-through-under sequences, contact lifts, and chair duets. Scott Graham was the co-director of the original production with Geordie Brookman, contributing movement direction specifically shaped around the Price family’s emotional dynamics.

What makes Frantic Assembly’s approach relevant to Things I Know to Be True specifically is their philosophical starting point: movement should communicate what words cannot. In the context of this play, this translates directly to the moments of greatest emotional intensity. When Bob and a child cannot speak to each other directly about what is happening, Bovell gives them a movement sequence instead. The sequence does not illustrate the conversation; it replaces it with something more honest. A chair duet between Bob and Rosie, for instance, might communicate across several minutes of movement everything that a two-page conversation between them could not.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly’s key techniques in this play: chair duets (two performers using chairs as contact-improvisation props, expressing relationship through shared weight and negotiated movement); lifts (one performer carrying or lifting another, expressing both protection and the effort of love); and round-by-through-under sequences (continuous, flowing movement through each other’s bodies, suggesting emotional entanglement). None of these are decorative; all are structurally placed to replace dialogue at the point where dialogue fails.

The Moment of Transition: Moving Between Registers

The most interesting theatrical moments in Things I Know to Be True are the transitions: the point where naturalistic dialogue ends and a movement sequence begins, or where a movement sequence dissolves back into dialogue. How does a company signal to the audience that the register is changing? And how does a designer support those transitions?

In production, these transitions are typically managed through a combination of sound, lighting and the performers’ own physical approach to stillness. The dialogue scene reaches its emotional peak — a phrase, a silence, a look — and then the movement begins, often initiated by a single performer before the others join. A sound designer might cue a shift in the soundscape: the domestic acoustic of the kitchen falls away and a non-diegetic, texturally abstract underscore takes its place. A lighting designer might allow the lighting state to shift slightly: the movement sequences often benefit from a reduction in overall intensity, with one or two moving lights following the performers, so that the space feels different — more interior, more subjective — than it does during the dialogue scenes. When the movement ends and dialogue resumes, the lighting returns, the soundscape resolves, and the audience is brought back to the domestic world they were in before.

Stanislavski’s system asks: what does this character want? What are their given circumstances? How does their past shape this moment? It starts from the inside — from the character’s inner life — and works outward to the physical expression of that inner life. The result, when it works, is a performance that appears effortlessly truthful: the words and the body seem to arise from the same source.

Frantic Assembly’s approach asks: what does this body do? How do two bodies relate to each other in space? What does shared weight communicate that words cannot? It starts from the outside — from physical contact and spatial relationship — and works inward. The performers are not asked to “feel something and show it”; they are asked to execute a precise physical task, and the feeling arises from the task. This is in some ways the inverse of Stanislavski’s method, yet in Things I Know to Be True the two approaches are placed alongside each other in the same production and the same family, and they reinforce rather than contradict each other. The Stanislavskian given circumstances of the Price family give the Frantic Assembly movement sequences their specific emotional charge; the movement sequences, in turn, reveal the subterranean emotional life that Stanislavskian truth keeps below the surface of the dialogue.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For any question that asks you to apply practitioner techniques to this play, you must do more than describe the practitioner’s biography. A good answer shows the technique applied to a specific moment of the set play. The pattern to follow is: name the practitioner, name the technique, name the moment in the play where it applies, and explain what the technique achieves for the audience at that moment. For example: “Frantic Assembly’s chair-duet technique could be applied to the moment when Bob and a child are unable to speak directly to each other — the shared weight and negotiated movement of the duet communicates the effort of their relationship without any dialogue needing to name it, creating an emotional honesty the naturalistic scene cannot reach.”

For a 20-mark response, use the performer or designer perspective named in the question. Explain how the chosen technique shapes the performance or design choices for a specific moment and affects the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Things I Know to Be True uses two traditions in deliberate combination: Stanislavskian acting for the naturalistic dialogue scenes (given circumstances, objectives, emotional truth) and Frantic Assembly physical theatre for the movement sequences (chair duets, lifts, round-by-through-under). Both are built into the structure, not added as decoration.
  • Stanislavski starts from the inside (inner life, given circumstances) and works outward; Frantic Assembly starts from the outside (physical task, shared weight) and works inward. In this play, the two approaches reinforce each other: Stanislavskian truth charges the movement with specific emotional meaning; the movement reveals what the dialogue keeps below the surface.
  • The transitions between registers — dialogue to movement, movement back to dialogue — are supported by sound and lighting design. A soundscape shift and a change in lighting state signal to the audience that the register has changed. Every transition is a design opportunity.

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Rosie in a Frantic Assembly movement sequence with Bob, explain the specific physical approach you would take to communicate the relationship between daughter and father. practice_questions.marks:
Top band: Specific physical choices for the Frantic Assembly sequence: weight-sharing described in detail (e.g. beginning with Rosie offering her weight to Bob and him accepting it, establishing a physical trust; later in the sequence, Bob initiating a lift that Rosie resists slightly before yielding, suggesting the complexity of the relationship); spatial proximity managed carefully (close enough to communicate intimacy; not so close that it becomes claustrophobic, preserving the sense that this is a father and daughter rather than two people in crisis); pace of movement: beginning slower and increasing as the sequence builds, then resolving to stillness, so that the emotional trajectory is felt in the body before it is understood by the mind. Every choice anchored to the specific emotional content of the father-daughter relationship.

Upper-mid band: At least two specific physical choices for the sequence with justification; both anchored to the father-daughter relationship; audience effect present. May not achieve the precision of Mastering.

Lower-mid band: General movement ideas (e.g. 'we would move slowly and carefully'); limited specificity; audience effect implied.

Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience's experience of the moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band: Specific lighting state described for the dialogue scene (e.g. a naturalistic interior warm wash, Fresnel cover from above, no moving lights, a sense of domestic ordinariness). Transition: a gradual dimming of the general wash (3-5 seconds) as the movement sequence begins, paired with the activation of one or two moving lights that track the performers, removing them from the fixed domestic world; gel shifts to a cooler, slightly less saturated tone (e.g. from warm 3000K to a neutral or slightly blue-tinted 4000K equivalent) to signal the shift to a more interior, subjective register. Return: the reverse at the sequence's end — the moving lights fade, the domestic wash returns, the gobo (if used for the garden) reinstates. Every choice explained with its effect on the audience.

Upper-mid band: At least two named lighting choices for the transition; both explained with audience effect; at least one named element (lantern type, gel colour, intensity). May not achieve the full precision of Mastering.

Lower-mid band: Lighting changes described in general terms ('I would dim the lights'); one or two choices; effect implied.

Low band: Mention of lighting with no specific elements; no clear link to the transition moment.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging a scene from Things I Know to Be True that uses both Stanislavskian naturalistic dialogue and a Frantic Assembly movement sequence, explain how you would direct the performers across both registers and how the design would support the transition between them. Refer to specific practitioner techniques, performer choices and at least two design disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band: Both practitioners addressed with specific techniques. Stanislavski: the performer is anchored in given circumstances for the dialogue scene (specific objective named, e.g. Bob trying to hold the family together; specific physical grounding, e.g. hands in the soil, a physical task that is then released at the emotional peak). Frantic Assembly: the movement sequence described with named vocabulary (round-by-through-under, shared weight, a lift); the emotional content the sequence communicates named and justified. Design: lighting state for dialogue vs movement sequence (specific choices per phase); soundscape transition (diegetic domestic sounds for the dialogue; abstract underscore for the movement; return to diegetic on resolution). Costume contributes to the reading of the movement (e.g. a fabric that moves well, or a contrast between a character who is dressed more formally and one who moves with greater physical freedom). Every choice justified with reference to audience effect.

Upper-mid band: Both practitioners addressed; at least two design disciplines; specific choices made with justification. May not achieve the full integration of Mastering.

Lower-mid band: Both practitioners mentioned but not applied to specific moments; design present but general; audience effect implied.

Low band: One practitioner only, or both practitioners described biographically without application to the staging task.

glossary_terms.definition: A theatrical style pioneered by Konstantin Stanislavski that seeks truthful, internally motivated performance, grounding character in specific given circumstances and emotional authenticity.

A form of theatre in which movement and physical expression are as important as, or more important than, spoken text, often using contact improvisation, ensemble dynamics and non-naturalistic gesture.
Stanislavski's term for all the information about a character's situation: who they are, where they are, when the scene takes place, and what has happened before.
Stanislavski's term for a goal a character pursues in a scene or moment.
A Frantic Assembly movement technique in which two or more performers pass through each other's bodies in a continuous flowing sequence, creating a sense of fluidity and emotional entanglement.
A Frantic Assembly technique in which two performers use chairs as contact-improvisation props to create a sequence of lifts, slides, counter-balances and shared weight.
A continuous ambient sound environment constructed from multiple elements, used to create place and emotional atmosphere.
The quality, colour and intensity of light on stage at a given moment, created by the combination of all active lanterns.
